name: K'iche', West Central
confidence_why: Henderson 2012, Larsen 1988, Baird 2015, Dürr 2004 and Bennett 2016 all place main stress on the final syllable of the word, with only a small class of exceptions where a light suffix pushes stress back onto the root, but none of them supports the alternating secondary stresses shown in the rule, and Henderson 2012 argues explicitly that K'ichee' does not build iambic feet.

new_statements.translation: p. 24: Word stress almost always falls on the last syllable. — p. 84: In present-day dialects of K'iche' stress has no phonemic status; it falls regularly on the last syllable of a word; only monosyllabic particles are normally unstressed. — p. 83: In some dialects unstressed vowels are partly deleted, e.g. kinaq' 'bean' is pronounced [knaqˀ] in Chichicastenango.
new_statements.citation: Dürr, Michael (2004). Einführung in das kolonialzeitliche Quiché (Kiche) : an Hand der Sprache des Popol Wuj. Freie Univ. vi+120 pp.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-phonemic and falls regularly on the final syllable of the word; monosyllabic particles are normally unstressed; unstressed (non-final) vowels can be deleted in some dialects.
new_statements.exceptions: 'fast immer' (almost always) on p. 24; monosyllabic particles normally unstressed (p. 84).
new_statements.identity_note: Dürr's course describes colonial 16th-century K'iche' as written in the Popol Wuj, but its stress statement on p. 84 is explicitly about present-day K'iche' dialects (heutige Dialekte), with a Chichicastenango vowel-deletion example; the p. 24 statement is the pronunciation guide for the reconstructed colonial forms. Brasseur 1862 describes 19th-century Quiché from colonial manuscripts, with Cakchiquel and Tzutuhil in parallel columns. The Dürr copy read is the 2015 revised edition (WS 2014/15), not the 2004 printing listed.

new_statements.quote: p. 28: In den heutigen Dialekten des Quiché hat die Betonung keinen Phonemstatus; sie fällt regelmäßig auf die letzte Silbe eines Wortes, nur einsilbige Partikeln sind teilweise unbetont (Nahualá: Mondloch 1978a: 9–10; Cantel: Fox 1965: 20).3 — fn. 3: Norman (1976: 56) gibt für Santa Catarina Ixtahuacán jedoch abweichend von Mondloch an, daß bei Worten mit auslautendem Kurzvokal die vorletzte Silbe betont sei. — p. 37: In allen Fällen handelt es sich bei der betroffenen Silbe um eine prätonische, überwiegend um die unmittelbar vor der Silbe stehende, die die Hauptbetonung trägt. — p. 2: Eine weitere Erscheinung ist die Tilgung von Kurzvokalen in prätonischen Silben.
new_statements.translation: p. 28: In the present-day dialects of Quiché, stress has no phonemic status; it falls regularly on the last syllable of a word, only monosyllabic particles are partly unstressed (Nahualá: Mondloch 1978a: 9-10; Cantel: Fox 1965: 20). — fn. 3: Norman (1976: 56), however, states for Santa Catarina Ixtahuacán, differing from Mondloch, that in words ending in a short vowel the penultimate syllable is stressed. — p. 37: In all cases [of vowel loss] the affected syllable is a pretonic one, mostly the one immediately before the syllable that carries the main stress. — p. 2: A further phenomenon [in modern dialects] is the deletion of short vowels in pretonic syllables.
new_statements.citation: Dürr, Michael (2003). Morphologie, Syntax und Textstrukturen des (Maya-)Quiche des Popol Vuh : linguistische Beschreibung eines kolonialzeitlichen Dokuments aus dem Hochland von Guatemala. Freie Univ.

new_statements.relation_note: Same primary placement as the catalog record (final syllable; catalog 'fixed-dominant alternating stress from the right) and essentially the same wording as the Dürr 2004 statement already held by the project; adds (a) explicit dialect attributions inside West Central K'iche' (Nahualá, Cantel), (b) the Santa Catarina Ixtahuacán exception for short-vowel-final words (Norman 1976), (c) pretonic short-vowel deletion. It gives no support for the alternating secondary stresses implied by the catalog grid (silent on secondary stress, like Larsen 1988 and Henderson 2012 held by the project).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and falls regularly on the final syllable of the word in the modern K'iche' dialects (documented for Nahualá and Cantel, both West Central); monosyllabic particles may be unstressed. The author states this for the modern dialects and assumes it for the colonial Quiché of the Popol Vuh, whose orthography does not show stress; pretonic short vowels tend to be deleted.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress (the term 'Hauptbetonung' on p. 37 implies a main stress but no secondary-stress pattern is described).
new_statements.exceptions: Monosyllabic particles are partly unstressed; fn. 3: Norman (1976: 56) reports for Santa Catarina Ixtahuacán that words ending in a short vowel stress the penultimate syllable (a dialect-specific deviation from Mondloch's Nahualá description).
new_statements.identity_note: Dürr 2003 describes the colonial Quiché of the Popol Vuh (16th c., Santa Cruz del Quiché / highland Guatemala) but its stress statement is explicitly about the present-day dialects, sourced to Nahualá (Mondloch 1978a) and Cantel (Fox 1965), both within Glottolog's West Central K'iche' (kich1266), with a footnote on Santa Catarina Ixtahuacán (Norman 1976), also West Central. Baird 2014 (unread) reportedly uses Nahualá speakers.

audit.recode_to: final stress (final primary, no secondary marks), classification fixed-dominant unchanged (Henderson's light-non-root exception sáqa/katéla, Baird fn.1 'minute number' of penult cases justify dominant-not-strict); and strike the kich1262 'variant fence' text claiming 'OKMA dialect surveys of K'iche' report final primary + alternating secondaries' -- the secondaries trace to Wikipedia, not OKMA. Since kich1266 is a retired code already aliased to kich1262 and rests on the identical Henderson quotation as kich1262/1263/1264/1265/1267, folding the row into kich1262 outright is the cleaner alternative.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote: confirmed verbatim at Henderson 2012 preprint p. 26 (82) in the copy downloaded now (record had no copies we hold). (2) Source: a 2012 NLLT phonology article with first-hand data partly from the West-Central area (Santa Lucía Utatlán ~ Nahualá); for primary stress it is a good source and agrees with Larsen 1988:21/fn.11 (held), Bennett 2016:495 and Baird 2015:165 (both downloaded): stress is word-final, with a small class of root-stressed exceptions before light non-root material. (3) The problem is the rule string. alternating stress from the right marks alternating secondary stresses leftward from the ultima. those Larsen pages are phoneme tables and Larsen
audit.second_reader_evidence: Independent re-check of every claim in the prior assessment; all confirmed. (1) QUOTE: (45-pp preprint, extracted text) p. 26, sec. 4.1, ex. (82) reads verbatim 'K'ICHEE' STRESS GENERALIZATION Stress falls on the final syllable of a prosodic word, unless that syllable is light non-root material, in which case it falls on the final root syllable.' followed by 'The first part of the generalization is that stress is attracted to the right edge of the prosodic word.' The sentence before (82) says it 'captures the distribution of primary stress in K'ichee''. p. 27: 'K'ichee' cannot be trochaic.
